source.title: Autoregulating Jump Performance to Induce Functional Overreaching

paper.citation: Claudino, J. G., Cronin, J. B., Mezêncio, B., Pinho, J. P., Pereira, C., Mochizuki, L., Amadio, A. C., & Serrão, J. C. (2016). Autoregulating jump performance to induce functional overreaching. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 30(8), 2242–2249. https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001325
paper.abstract: Can individualized minimal-difference thresholds in CMJ height regulate training load to produce a planned overreaching response and post-taper rebound in youth team-sport athletes? Eighteen national-level male U17 futsal players (mean age 15.2 years) were randomized to regulated or preplanned training groups of nine. The six-week protocol comprised four intensified weeks and a two-week stepped taper. Results reflect one small adolescent male futsal cohort rather than adult collegiate American football. Participants completed CMJ familiarization and two reliability sessions; each athlete's typical error and 95% confidence interval defined the minimal individual difference. The regulated group had weekly training volume adjusted when mean height from eight CMJs differed from the planned response; the control group followed preplanned training. CMJ height was assessed at baseline, after four intensified weeks, and after the two-week taper; session-RPE captured another dimension of load. Group-by-time effects used two-way ANOVA with small-sample-adjusted effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals.
paper.tldr: This small randomized trial tests a concrete method for adjusting training volume from an athlete's countermovement-jump response during a deliberately intensified and tapered block. Regulated-group load was 8.2% and 14.5% higher than control in weeks 3 and 4 (p<.001); total load rose 56% across intensification in the regulated group versus 48% in control. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Participants completed CMJ familiarization and two reliability sessions; each athlete's typical error and 95% confidence interval defined the minimal individual difference. The regulated group had weekly training volume adjusted when mean height from eight CMJs differed from the planned response; the control group followed preplanned training. CMJ height was assessed at baseline, after four intensified weeks, and after the two-week taper; session-RPE captured another dimension of load. Group-by-time effects used two-way ANOVA with small-sample-adjusted effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals.
paper.findings: Regulated-group load was 8.2% and 14.5% higher than control in weeks 3 and 4 (p<.001); total load rose 56% across intensification in the regulated group versus 48% in control. At the end of intensification, regulated-group CMJ height decreased with an effect size of -0.31 (95% CI -0.58 to -0.02), while the control change was not significant. After taper, regulated-group CMJ height exceeded baseline with an effect size of 0.30 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.51); the control-group change remained non-significant. Final training load did not differ significantly between groups (p=.082), so the observed performance difference arose within a short, adaptive protocol rather than a persistent between-group load separation.
paper.limitations: Nine athletes per group produce imprecise estimates and make the result vulnerable to baseline imbalance and individual responders. Biological and training age constrain transfer beyond similarly trained adolescents. Nutrition was not controlled, and non-disclosure of jump feedback may have increased measurement error. CMJ height was both the decision signal and primary performance outcome; no independent sport-performance or health outcome established broader benefit. Deliberately inducing performance suppression is not inherently safe or appropriate, and the study does not validate injury-risk or readiness thresholds.
paper.practicalImplications: The useful principle is to predefine measurement error and decision rules before modifying load, then judge the athlete's response against the intended phase objective. Do not copy the exact thresholds or attempt deliberate overreaching from this small youth sample. Pair CMJ data with exposure, symptoms, wellness, maturation, and coaching context, and use conservative stop rules.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, the useful principle is to predefine measurement error and decision rules before modifying load, then judge the athlete's response against the intended phase objective. Do not copy the exact thresholds or attempt deliberate overreaching from this small youth sample. Pair CMJ data with exposure, symptoms, wellness, maturation, and coaching context, and use conservative stop rules. Preserve the study population and avoid converting one finding into a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
